source: “Haul in the chains! Let the carcase go astern!”

The vast tackles have now done their duty. The peeled white body of the beheaded whale flashes like a marble sepulchre; though changed in hue, it has not perceptibly lost anything in bulk. It is still colossal. Slowly it floats more and more away, the water round it torn and splashed by the insatiate sharks, and the air above vexed with rapacious flights of screaming fowls, whose beaks are like so many insulting poniards in the whale. The vast white headless phantom floats further and further from the ship, and every rod that it so floats, what seem square roods of sharks and cubic roods of fowls, augment the murderous din. For hours and hours from the almost stationary ship that hideous sight is seen. Beneath the unclouded and mild azure sky, upon the fair face of the pleasant sea, wafted by the joyous breezes, that great mass of death floats on and on, till lost in infinite perspectives.

There’s a most doleful and most mocking funeral! The sea-vultures all in pious mourning, the air-sharks all punctiliously in black or speckled. In life but few of them would have helped the whale, I ween, if peradventure he had needed it; but upon the banquet of his funeral they most piously do pounce. Oh, horrible vultureism of earth! from which not the mightiest whale is free.

Nor is this the end. Desecrated as the body is, a vengeful ghost survives and hovers over it to scare. Espied by some timid man-of-war or blundering discovery-vessel from afar, when the distance obscuring the swarming fowls, nevertheless still shows the white mass floating in the sun, and the white spray heaving high against it; straightway the whale’s unharming corpse, with trembling fingers is set down in the log—shoals, rocks, and breakers hereabouts: beware! And for years afterwards, perhaps, ships shun the place; leaping over it as silly sheep leap over a vacuum, because their leader originally leaped there when a stick was held. There’s your law of precedents; there’s your utility of traditions; there’s the story of your obstinate survival of old beliefs never bottomed on the earth, and now not even hovering in the air! There’s orthodoxy!
Thus, while in life the great whale’s body may have been a real terror to his foes, in his death his ghost becomes a powerless panic to a world.
Are you a believer in ghosts, my friend? There are other ghosts than the Cock-Lane one, and far deeper men than Doctor Johnson who believe in them.

modern_en.title: Chapter 69 — The Funeral
paragraphs: "Haul in the chains! Let the carcass go astern!"

The vast tackles have now done their duty. The peeled white body of the beheaded whale gleams like a marble tomb; though changed in color, it has not visibly lost anything in bulk. It is still colossal. Slowly it floats farther and farther away, the water around it torn and splashed by the insatiable sharks, and the air above harassed by rapacious flights of screaming birds, whose beaks are like so many insulting daggers in the whale. The vast white headless phantom floats farther and farther from the ship, and with every rod that it floats, what seem square roods of sharks and cubic roods of birds swell the murderous din. For hours and hours that hideous sight can be seen from the almost motionless ship. Beneath the unclouded, mild blue sky, upon the fair face of the pleasant sea, carried along by the joyous breezes, that great mass of death floats on and on, till it is lost in infinite perspectives.

What a doleful and mocking funeral this is! The sea-vultures all in pious mourning, the air-sharks all correctly dressed in black or speckled. Few of them, I suspect, would have lifted a finger for the whale in life, had he happened to need it; but at the banquet of his funeral they pounce with the greatest piety. Oh, the horrible vultureism of the earth, from which not even the mightiest whale is exempt!

Nor is this the end. Desecrated as the body is, a vengeful ghost survives and hovers over it to frighten. Sighted from afar by some timid warship or blundering discovery-vessel — when the distance hides the swarming birds but still shows the white mass floating in the sun, and the white spray heaving high against it — straightaway the whale's harmless corpse is set down in the log with trembling fingers: "Shoals, rocks, and breakers hereabouts: beware!" And for years afterward, perhaps, ships avoid the place, leaping over it as silly sheep leap over empty air, because their leader originally leaped there when a stick was held up. There's your law of precedents; there's your usefulness of traditions; there's the story of your stubborn survival of old beliefs never grounded on the earth, and now not even hovering in the air! There's orthodoxy!
So while the great whale's living body may have been a real terror to his enemies, once he is dead his ghost becomes a powerless panic to a whole world.
Do you believe in ghosts, my friend? There are other ghosts besides the Cock-Lane one (the famous London ghost hoax of 1762), and men far deeper than Doctor Johnson believe in them.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 69 — Begravelsen
paragraphs: »Hal kæderne ind! Lad slagtekroppen gå agterud!«

De vældige taljer har nu gjort deres pligt. Den flåede, hvide krop af den hovedløse hval skinner som en marmorgrav. Selv om farven er ændret, har den ikke synligt mistet noget af sit omfang. Den er stadig kolossal. Langsomt driver den længere og længere væk, mens vandet omkring den bliver revet og pjasket af de umættelige hajer, og luften over den bliver plaget af grådige flokke skrigende fugle, hvis næb er som så mange fornærmende dolke i hvalen. Det vældige hvide hovedløse genfærd driver længere og længere fra skibet, og for hver stang, det driver, svulmer det, der ligner kvadratstænger af hajer og kubikstænger af fugle, det morderiske spektakel. I timevis kan man se det hæslige syn fra det næsten ubevægelige skib. Under den skyfri, milde blå himmel, på det smukke ansigt af det behagelige hav, båret af de glade vinde, driver den store dødsmasse videre og videre, indtil den taber sig i uendelige perspektiver.

Sikke en sørgelig og hånlig begravelse! Havets gribbe er alle i from sorg, luftens hajer alle korrekt klædt i sort eller spættet. Få af dem ville, tror jeg, have løftet en finger for hvalen, mens den levede, hvis den havde behøvet det. Men ved hans begravelsesfest kaster de sig over ham med den største fromhed. O, jordens skrækkelige gribbeskab, som ikke engang den mægtigste hval er fri for!

Og det er ikke enden. Hvor vanhelliget kroppen end er, overlever et hævngerrigt genfærd og svæver over den for at skræmme. Når et frygtsomt krigsskib eller et famlende opdagelsesskib får øje på den på afstand — når afstanden skjuler de myldrende fugle, men stadig viser den hvide masse flydende i solen og det hvide skumsprøjt, der hæver sig højt mod den — så bliver hvalens uskadelige lig straks skrevet ind i logbogen med rystende fingre: »Grunde, klipper og brændinger her omkring: Pas på!« Og i årevis efter holder skibene måske uden om stedet og springer over det, som dumme får springer over tom luft, fordi deres leder oprindelig sprang der, da man holdt en stok op. Der har du din lov om præcedens, der har du traditionernes nytte, der har du historien om din stædige overlevelse af gamle overbevisninger, der aldrig var grundet på jorden og nu ikke engang svæver i luften! Der har du ortodoksien!
Så selv om den store hvals levende krop kan have været en virkelig rædsel for hans fjender, bliver hans genfærd, når han er død, til en magtesløs panik for en hel verden.
Tror du på genfærd, min ven? Der findes andre genfærd end det i Cock Lane (den berømte londonske spøgelsessvindel fra 1762), og mænd, der er langt dybere end doktor Johnson, tror på dem.
